runs.analysis: Candidates A and B appear to be identical, word for word, across all nine sections (Purpose through Review Assumptions). Both use the same deterministic "# Title\n\ncontent" structure, and both are complete with no truncation. I found no differences in faithfulness, specificity, correctness or fitness for downstream stages, so neither is better.

Candidates A and B appear textually identical. Both contain the same nine documents in order, each under a "# <Title>" heading. The content, numbers and structure match section by section, and neither is truncated or altered. Neither has an advantage on faithfulness, specificity, correctness, format or downstream usefulness.

Both candidates are complete, cover all nine documents in order, and keep the key facts: €40B, 100 m, Spain–Morocco, EUR/MAD, the 18 risks and the 7 review issues. The difference is how well each follows the stage's heading rules. The prompt tweak says to keep the wording and level of existing '#'/'##' headings and to turn section-label lines such as "Rationale:" into '##' headings.

Candidate A keeps most original headings and wording, for example "# Disciplines this project involves", "# Requirements for physical locations" and "# Domain of the expert reviewer". In Make Assumptions it keeps the "Assumptions:" block and a separate "## ... Assessment" heading for each question, plus the Recommendation line. It is also more compact in the risk section. Its weaknesses are a duplicated "# Purpose" line, labels such as "Impact:" and "Likelihood:" left as plain lines instead of '##' headings, and Review Assumptions that are only lightly condensed. Some details are dropped, such as the electrification standards in Issue 5.

Candidate B renames and restructures headings: "Physical Location Requirement", "Physical Locations Plan", "Disciplines" instead of the original title, "Domain of the Expert Reviewer" recapitalised, and Distill sections regrouped. It also changes spellings such as "geotechnic". It collapses each Make Assumptions question into dense bullets with inline "Financial Feasibility Assessment:" labels. That is the opposite of turning label lines into '##' headings, and it makes the section harder to scan. Its risk section is longer and barely shortened. On the plus side, it retains more detail in the review issues, such as the electrification standards and the earthquake probabilities.

A follows the heading-preservation and label-to-heading instructions better and is more compact. B has slightly richer detail but breaks the structure the tweak was meant to protect. A is modestly better.

Both candidates keep all nine documents in the right order and preserve the key facts: €40B, 20 years, Strait of Gibraltar, 100m depth, EUR/MAD, the 18 risks, and the 7 review issues. Neither has factual contradictions, truncation or a "Problem with document" chunk. They differ in heading handling, which the prompt tweak targets, and in how much they shorten.

Heading levels and wording:
- A keeps the original sub-heading levels, such as "## Risk N", "## Question N", "## Location N" and "## Issue N". Each document therefore sits cleanly under its "# Title". A does promote "Topic" to "#" in Purpose and "Primary Domain" to "#" in Domain. It also adds "Disciplines" and "Risk summary" headings, which may differ slightly from the originals.
- B promotes Risks, Questions, and the Review's "Domain of the expert reviewer" to "#". It also lowercases some wording ("Domain of the expert reviewer", "Review conclusion") and renames headings ("Disciplines this project involves"). This is the heading promotion and renaming the tweak was meant to stop. It also flattens the hierarchy, because every risk and question becomes a peer of the document title.

Section label lines:
- B turns the assessment labels in Make Assumptions into "##" headings ("Financial Feasibility Assessment", and so on). However, it leaves "Assumptions:" and "Recommendation:" as plain label lines.
- A collapses each Make Assumptions question into bullets and drops the assessment headings. That loses structure the tweak wanted to keep.

Shortening:
- A is barely shortened in the Risks and Review sections. It keeps nearly all of the full text.
- B compresses more, especially in Risks (for example, Risk 8 loses the MAD appreciation point). It does not compress the Make Assumptions section at all. It also keeps more prose.
- B is somewhat closer to a "short" version. A's Make Assumptions is much shorter than B's, though, so overall length is mixed.

Overall A is slightly more faithful on heading levels, which matters for downstream parsing. B is slightly better on assessment-heading conversion. The two are close.

The two candidates look identical. I compared every section: Purpose, Domain, Plan Type, Physical Locations, Currency Strategy, Identify Risks, Make Assumptions, Distill Assumptions and Review Assumptions. I found no differences in wording, numbers or structure. Both use the deterministic `# <Title>\n\n<content>` format with all nine documents in order, and neither is truncated. Both share the same weaknesses. They carry upstream content that conflicts with the plan prompt. Examples are the 80% buffer / 20% buildable model, the 60% tenant threshold where the prompt says 30–50%, and the "hyper-dense" framing. But a deterministic merge should reproduce its inputs, so these flaws do not separate the candidates.

Candidates A and B appear to be identical, character for character. Both have the same nine documents in the same order, with the same "# Title" headings and the same content. They follow the deterministic full-merge format equally well, and neither has truncation, omissions or added text. Any problems, such as the Distill Assumptions bullets or the Make Assumptions numbers, affect both equally. No criterion separates them.

Candidate A is more compressed. It keeps the original-looking heading levels ("## Risk n", "## Question n", "## Location n"), which fits the prompt tweak to preserve heading levels. It has several defects. The Domain table is broken: a header row with no rows, followed by pipe-delimited bullets. Q3 now says "Commitments must be non-binding to maintain efficacy", which inverts the meaning, since non-binding commitments lose efficacy. Unresolved "Decision N / Choice N" cross-references remain in the risks and review sections, and a downstream reader can't resolve them. The Purpose and Domain sections are very thin. Some qualifiers are lost, such as "Phase 0 remediation" and "near Dunkirk" for the heat-reuse partner.

Candidate B keeps more of the substantive content and reads cleanly. It mostly removes the dangling "Decision N" references. It preserves the Q3 meaning correctly. It keeps useful detail: the 50-70 km cluster separation, the €257.6M holding-cost figure, and the heat-reuse partner near Dunkirk. Its main weakness is heading handling. Many "##" headings were promoted to "#" (Risk n, Question n), and some titles were rewritten (Purpose now carries the project title as its "#" heading). This goes against the prompt tweak. The Distill section loses its subheadings and becomes a flat list. The "€257.6M over 5 years" figure looks slightly off, since that is the annual figure, but it appears to come from the upstream text.

Overall, A follows the heading-preservation rule better. B is more accurate and complete in content, with no meaning inversion and no broken table, and it is more usable downstream. I weight B's content quality slightly above A's formatting fidelity, but the margin is small.

Stage is the "short" variant. A keeps more substance, mostly preserves the original heading wording, and turns label lines such as "Rationale" into '##' headings, as instructed. It has a few odd promotions, such as "# Primary Domain: …", and one numeric slip: €257.6M is stated "over 5 years" when it is the per-year figure. B compresses more but renames headings ("Project Plan Summary", "Project Classification"), leaves a malformed empty table in the Domain section, and flips the meaning of Q3 with "Commitments must be non-binding to maintain efficacy". It also regroups the Distill items and keeps dangling "Decision X" references to documents not included. A is more faithful and more useful downstream, and B's semantic reversal and formatting problems are worse than A's single slip.

Candidates A and B look identical, with the same content in every section: Purpose, Domain, Plan Type, Physical Locations, Currency, Risks, Assumptions, Distill, and Review. I found no differences in wording, structure or completeness. Neither is better on any criterion.
Candidates A and B appear to be identical, word for word. Both include all nine upstream documents in the correct order, with the same headings and content, so I found no difference on any criterion.

Candidate A keeps the sub-document headings at "##" level (Risk N, Question N, Location N, Issue N), as the prompt tweak requires. It compresses each document into bullets and keeps all the key numbers and decisions. It converts some labels such as Rationale into "##" headings, but not in Physical Locations. It has minor typos and one garbled sentence in the risk summary. Candidate B has cleaner prose and keeps a few extra details. However, it promotes Risk and Question headings to "#", which is the promotion the tweak was meant to prevent, so its hierarchy is inconsistent. It is also less condensed, closer to a light paraphrase than a short version. Overall A follows the stage's instructions better.

Both candidates cover all nine documents, and both are complete and consistent with the plan. The difference is in how well each follows the shortening rules (keep the existing headings, turn label lines into '##' headings) and how much decision-useful detail each keeps.

Candidate A mostly keeps the apparent original headings. These include 'Primary domain: Financial Clearing Mechanisms', 'This plan requires one or more physical locations…', and the Distill section headings. It also turns the assessment label lines in Make Assumptions into '##' headings, such as '## Financial Mechanism Viability Assessment', which is what the tweak asks for. It keeps more concrete detail, such as the 20% safety-buffer example in Risk 3, the full-sentence Impact/Likelihood/Severity/Action lines, and the Currency rationale. Its flaws are the duplicated '# Purpose' heading and the unconverted 'Business:' label. It also appears to promote the 'Risk N' and 'Question N' headings to '#' (probably from '##'), which is the promotion problem the tweak was meant to prevent.

Candidate B keeps '## Risk N' and '## Question N' at what is probably the original level. However, it appears to invent or rename several top-level headings: 'Project Structure Summary', 'Project Planning Summary', and the Purpose title, which is taken from the Topic. It also rewrites content heavily into terse bullets and re-organises the Distill section. It leaves 'Title:' bullets instead of '##' headings. It does not convert the 'Assumptions:' and 'Assessments:' labels into '##' headings either. It drops some detail, such as the 20% buffer example. It contains a typo ('Monitioring'), a broken sentence ('unreliable data functional failure'), and a redundant Currency section. The Make Assumptions section repeats itself.

Overall, A is somewhat more faithful to the original wording and detail and handles the label-to-heading conversion better. B is better on the Risk and Question heading levels but renames headings and compresses away useful specifics.

Candidates A and B are identical. Both contain the same nine documents in the same order, with the same headings and content. I found no differences in faithfulness, completeness, structure or consistency. Both carry the same upstream flaws, such as Leipzig's population of about 616k exceeding the 150k–400k range. Neither candidate has an edge.

After comparing the two candidates section by section, I found no differences. Both contain the same nine documents in the same order. The headings, content and formatting match. Both are the full deterministic concatenation in the format `# <Title>\n\n<content>`. Both carry the same upstream flaws: Leipzig's population of about 616k is outside the 150k–400k target, and the Distill Assumptions bullet "Night < 19°C" contradicts the "Nighttime Minimum > 19°C" assumption. Neither candidate fixes or worsens these, so they are equal on every criterion.

**Candidate A**
- It keeps the upstream heading levels and wording. Examples are "# Question 1 - …", "# Risk 1 - …" and "## Assumptions". This follows the prompt tweak to keep existing '#'/'##' headings.
- It keeps nearly all the substance. That includes the mitigation actions in the risks and the full assumption rationales. Those are useful for later stages.
- It is barely shortened, so it is weaker as a "short" version.
- It turns the "Rationale:" labels in the Locations section into plain prose, not '##' headings. That is a minor deviation.
- It carries upstream flaws, such as "narrowly beating Public Health" and the "Night < 19°C" threshold wording. B has the same flaws.

**Candidate B**
- It is genuinely condensed and bulleted, which fits the "short" intent.
- It breaks the heading instructions the prompt tweak was written to enforce:
  - It renames headings: "Primary domain…" becomes "Project Planning Summary", and "This plan requires one or more physical locations…" becomes "Project Location Requirement".
  - It demotes heading levels: "# Question N" and "# Risk N" become "## Question N" and "## Risk N". It also rewrites the question titles as short labels.
  - It leaves "Rationale:" inline in the Locations section, not as '##' headings.
- It loses material detail. For example, the risk-mitigation text is truncated.
- It introduces some garbling in Review Issue 3: "contracted installation model (Decision 7, Option 2)" repeats the same option for both mechanisms. It also says "contradicts goal of isolating social housing protection", which is incoherent.

**Overall**
- B is more compact. It disregards the specific heading-preservation instructions and loses some content and clarity.
- A is more faithful to the stage's structural requirements and gives downstream stages more usable detail, even though its compression is light.
- A is better overall, but not by a large margin.

**Stage fit.** This is the "short" variant, so each upstream document should be shortened while keeping the wording and level of its existing headings. Section label lines such as "Rationale:" or "Assumptions:" should become '##' headings.

**Candidate A**
- It actually shortens the documents, using compact bullets.
- It keeps the heading levels from the upstream style: "## Risk 1 - …", "## Question 1 - …", "## Location 1", "## Issue 1 - …".
- It keeps the key decision-useful content: the 60/40 funding split; T+6 weeks for Tier 1 centers; 10 centers (42 staff) plus 10 outreach teams (20 staff); the 30°C/19°C thresholds; the CRM cost of €30k; the 15% contingency reserve of €300k; the sensitivity figures.
- It loses some nuance. The full Question text is gone, as are some opportunity and benefit statements, and the "3 people per shift, 14 hours/day" detail. These are minor losses for a reference document.
- It does not convert "Rationale:" or "Assumptions:" labels into '##' headings, so it only partly follows the tweak.

**Candidate B**
- It is barely shortened. Risks, questions and review issues are nearly verbatim.
- It promotes headings against the instruction. "## Risk n" becomes "# Risk n", "## Question n" becomes "# Question n - <long question text>", and the domain title becomes "# Primary domain: …". This is the heading-promotion behaviour the prompt tweak was meant to prevent.
- It drops the "Rationale"/"Assumptions" labels instead of turning them into headings.
- It keeps more detail, which helps downstream stages, and a few of its additions are slightly more informative: 14 hours/day at 3 staff per shift; the landlord/tenant constraint on installations; Leipzig's hot-night trend.
- That extra detail comes mostly at the cost of the stage's purpose, which is a shortened reference.

**Shared flaws.** Both carry upstream errors: "Night < 19°C" in the distilled assumptions, which contradicts the "Night Min > 19°C" trigger in the Make Assumptions section; "Decision 7, Option 2" appearing twice in Issue 3; and Leipzig (~616k) being outside the 150k–400k brief. Neither candidate fixes these.

**Verdict.** A is better aligned with the short-variant purpose and the heading-preservation rule, while keeping the essential facts. B is more informative but largely ignores the shortening goal and violates the heading-level rule.
